title: Pencil notes, never retype the page
allegory: A residual block is like an editor who pencils notes onto the page and passes page plus notes along, instead of retyping the whole thing; with nothing to add, the page goes through untouched.
map: the page handed down the line
F = 0: the block is the identity
complaints travelling back along the page itself
the gradient riding the skip path (the + passes it straight through)
credit: The 'gradient superhighway' framing of the skip path is borrowed from Andrej Karpathy, Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.

chapters.name: Deeper got worse
chapters.note: 56 layers did worse than 20, on training data

cap.1: A strange result: a 56-layer network did worse than a 20-layer one, even on data it had already seen. More layers should never make you worse. So what broke?
cap.2: On CIFAR-10, He et al. found a 56-layer plain net with higher training error than a 20-layer one. Not overfitting: the deep net could copy the shallow one by making its extra layers the identity. It just couldn't learn to.
cap.3: The degradation problem: deeper plain nets reach higher training error. The deep net's function class contains the shallow one's (extra layers = identity), so this is an optimisation failure, not capacity or overfitting.

cap.1: A plain network is a chain of typists, each retyping the whole page from scratch. Even exact copying must be learned, and fifty-six of them garble it.
cap.2: Each plain layer must produce its entire output anew. Leaving the signal alone means a stack of convs and ReLUs must learn the identity exactly, and gradient descent struggles to find it.
cap.3: A plain block maps x to H(x) directly, so H = identity has to be built out of nonlinear layers. Representable, but hard for the optimiser to reach: hence degradation.

cap.1: Now each editor pencils a few notes on the page and passes page plus notes along. Nothing to add? Pass it on untouched. Doing nothing is now easy.
cap.2: A residual block computes a correction F(x) and returns F(x) + x. To do nothing it only needs F = 0, and zero is easy to learn. Each block nudges the signal instead of rebuilding it.
cap.3: Reparameterise H(x) = F(x) + x. The identity is now F = 0, the natural resting point for layers under weight decay, so each block learns a residual: a correction to its input.

cap.1: The whole idea is one plus sign. The page goes through as it is, and the block's notes are added on top.
cap.2: F is two 3x3 convs, each followed by batchnorm, with a ReLU between them. The + x has no weights at all. When F outputs zeros, the block hands its input straight on.
cap.3: Basic block: F = conv3x3, BN, ReLU, conv3x3, BN; add the shortcut, then ReLU. The shortcut is parameter-free while shape and stride are unchanged.

cap.1: When the final result is wrong, the blame runs back along the page itself and reaches every editor directly, not through a long chain of retypings.
cap.2: A + node passes its gradient unchanged to both inputs. So the loss's gradient rides the skip path straight back through every block, forking into each F on the way.
cap.3: ∂(x + F(x))/∂x = I + ∂F/∂x. Chained over blocks, the identity terms give a path from the loss to early layers that skips every F, which is why vanishing gradients ease.

chapters.name: When shapes change
chapters.verdict: You can only add things of the same shape: resize the page, not the notes.

cap.1: When a block shrinks the page, the original no longer lines up with the notes. So the original is photocopied down to size first, then the two are added.
cap.2: Adding x to F(x) needs matching shapes. When the first block of a group downsamples with stride 2, the skip branch gets its own 1x1 stride-2 conv plus batchnorm; later blocks use a bare identity.
cap.3: In each BlockGroup the first block has stride 2 and a projection shortcut (1x1 conv, stride 2, BN); the rest keep identity shortcuts. Addition, unlike concatenation, demands exact shape agreement.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The transformer residual stream is this sum
Doing nothing must be the easy default

cap.1: Adding the input back let networks go deep. In transformers the same sum becomes a shared notepad every layer writes on, the place interpretability reads.
cap.2: ResNets reached 152 layers and won ILSVRC 2015 with this one addition. Chapter 1's residual stream is the same sum: every layer adds its notes, so you can read what each one wrote.
cap.3: Because the stream is a sum of block outputs, contributions decompose additively. Direct logit attribution and steering vectors rely on exactly that when you study and steer transformers.

coda.title: Top row: plain layers. Bottom row: residual blocks. Tap a cell to rest that layer (weights at zero).

caption.1: Tap a few cells to rest those layers. One resting plain layer wipes out the signal. Resting residual blocks just pass the page on.
caption.2: A resting layer has zero weights. Plain: it outputs 0 and everything after it is lost, gradients included. Residual: F = 0 makes the block the identity, so the signal survives.
caption.3: Toy linear chain: each active layer scales by 1.1. Plain output is the product of gains, 0 if any layer rests; residual is the product of (1 + F′), which is 1 for a resting block. Same logic as zero-ablating a transformer block.

where_else: The transformer residual stream: every attention head and MLP adds its output to one running sum
Zero-ablating a block in interpretability: the stream survives because the block only ever added to it
LoRA fine-tuning: learn a small update added to frozen weights, starting from zero

hamming.what: A block that learns a correction F(x) and adds it to its own input, so it outputs x + F(x).
hamming.when: Whenever you stack many layers: ResNets for images, and the residual stream of every transformer.
hamming.why: Doing nothing becomes the easy default and gradients get a direct path back, so very deep networks actually train.
